text: Padre Manuel Nunes (1848–1892), parish priest of São Gonçalo, noted preacher and satirical poet.
D. António Manuel Pereira Ribeiro, 28th bishop of Funchal from 1915, previously canon, teacher and capitular vicar in Funchal.

Biography of Dr Francisco Justino Gonçalves de Andrade (1821–1902), a native of Campanário who emigrated to Brazil and became professor of civil law at the São Paulo Faculty of Law, regarded as the foremost Brazilian civil lawyer of his day.
Perennial madder plant whose roots Madeirans used to dye cloth red and which was recommended against rickets.

A former square in Funchal, earlier called Passeio Público, renamed Praça da Constituição after the liberal constitution was proclaimed there on 28 January 1821. It became Praça da República in 1911 and disappeared in 1914 when the Avenida Oeste (now Avenida Dr. Manuel de Arriaga) was built.
German bryologist who collected mosses in Madeira in early 1912 and published a study of the moss flora of Madeira and Tenerife.
Records the measurements of magnetic inclination (dip) taken in Funchal between 1839 and 1906, showing a steady decrease over the period.
Redshank (Polygonum persicaria), a knotweed abundant in Madeira's pools and damp places.

Describes how the Constitutional Charter of 1826 and the restored liberal regime of 1834 were proclaimed in Madeira, focusing on the events of 3–6 June 1834 in Funchal. It records the people involved and the later yearly commemorations.
A Madeiran judicial bulletin whose first issue appeared in 1877.
A decapod crustacean occasionally caught in Madeiran waters.
Lisbon physician and medical professor who attended Princess Maria Amélia in Madeira in 1852–53, helped found the Princess's hospice and wrote a valued study of Funchal's climate and tuberculosis.
Vernacular name of Silene venosa, a plant of the pink family, not rare in Madeira and Porto Santo.
Dr Schmeller, author of an 1845 Munich study of Valentim Fernandes and his collection of reports on Portuguese discoveries.

Account of the two cholera epidemics in Madeira: the catastrophic outbreak of July–October 1856, brought by an infantry regiment from Lisbon and officially killing 7,041 people (reputedly about 10,000), and the far milder epidemic of 1910–1911, which killed 556 under the direction of Dr Carlos França.
Politician born in Vila Real in 1844, elected deputy for Madeira for 1892–93, who died in office in 1893.
The steamer Tornado, captured in Madeiran waters by the Spanish frigate Gerona in 1866 and taken to Cádiz.
Note on the Couto family name in Madeira, probably descended from Joane Anes de Couto Cardoso, landholder at Paul do Mar and Jardim do Mar.

Describes the landing place of Ribeira Brava, a pebble beach where embarking was difficult, and the quay built there between 1904 and 1908, linked to the town by a tunnel and a short road and served by coastal steamers.
The solemn vow, made after the great flood of 9 October 1803, placing Madeira and Funchal under the protection of the Virgin, specifically Nossa Senhora do Monte, and the annual feast that resulted.
Describes the vara de salto, a pole-and-line fishing implement used to catch skipjack and tuna.
Cross-reference: Berta de Ataíde is treated under D. Maria Helena Jervis de Atouguia e Almeida.
Lino Cassiano Jardim, physician from Santana trained at the Funchal Medical School, who qualified to practise in Brazil with a thesis on bilious fever (1871).
A grunt fish found on rocky bottoms off Madeira, named for the noises it makes when caught.

Discusses Plato's legendary Atlantis and later scientific theories of a sunken Atlantic continent, concluding that Madeira and its neighbouring islands are an independent volcanic creation rather than remnants of submerged land.
Portuguese writer who published a poem praising Madeira in 1898 and had visited Funchal in his youth to study documents.
The French frigate Belle Poule called at Funchal in July 1840 carrying the Prince de Joinville's mission to retrieve Napoleon's remains from St Helena.
A work published in Funchal in 1879 by the Sociedade da Primeira Gente do Mundo, a group of six authors who met at Desterro, Monte.
Bicho vaca is the local name for two millipedes of the genus Julus found in damp soil, pots and walls.
Biographical note on João da Camara Pestana, Funchal-born agronomist, Director-General of Agriculture, deputy for Madeira and later senator, who published on plant diseases and pests.

Short article on the spontaneous popular verse produced in Madeira during moments of public passion, above all the flood of pamphlet poems and satires published during the so-called Plague of the Lazaretto (1905–06). It lists many of these titles and deplores their excesses.

Biography of Dr Luiz Vicente de Afonseca (1803–1878), a Madeiran physician who served as deputy for Madeira in the Portuguese parliament for 34 years and was revered for his selfless defence of the archipelago's interests.
Biography of Manuel Pestana dos Reis (b. 1894), a Madeiran law graduate and poet who published the verse collection Canções de Tristes in 1913.
The Delgado surname, descending from early settlers Pedro Delgado and Isabel Fernandes who held land at Ponta do Sol.
Ernesto Jardim de Vilhena was a deputy for Madeira in the Portuguese parliament during the 1908–1910 session.

Brief biography of João Maria de Abreu Castelo Branco Cardoso e Melo, 1st Viscount and 1st Count of Fornos de Algodres, who served as civil governor of the Funchal district for about a year from 1852.
An animal-welfare society founded in Funchal in 1897 and declared of public utility in 1914; an earlier society of the same name was set up in 1880.
The entry lists his published works between 1787 and 1809. It adds that his impoverished daughter later received a state allowance.

Madeira received a seat in the Cortes in 1645, reportedly because it was the first possession to acclaim João IV. After 1820 the island elected deputies to the constitutional assemblies, interrupted by absolutist restorations until 1834.

A quoted passage praises the natural beauty of Madeira's valleys. It describes five in particular: Machico, Funchal with Vale Formoso, Jardim da Serra, São Vicente and the valley around Penha de Águia.
Describes the smallpox outbreaks of 1815, 1872–73 and 1907, their origins and death tolls, and how vaccination and isolation later limited the disease.

From 1849 the hospital occupied a house in the rua da Rochinha de Baixo until 1938. The site was ceded for the lyceum in 1936, and from November 1938 military patients were admitted to the Hospital dos Marmeleiros.

The text is taken from a 1908 newspaper study by Carlos de Meneses. Phylloxera has badly damaged Porto Santo's vines, and resistant American vine species are recommended for the island's limestone soils.

A table lists the Junta's revenues from 1902 to 1939. The revenue funded a new road network on an island that had only nine kilometres of good road in 1901, and the Junta's offices moved from the old Seminary of the Incarnation to the former Hospital of Santa Isabel.

Born in Funchal in 1778, he inherited from his brother a vast collection of entailed estates, making him Madeira's richest proprietor. He lived modestly and used his fortune to relieve crises and protect poor farmers from wine merchants.

Revenue figures for the Madeira customs houses from 1581–1587, 1748, 1812–1840 and 1896–1932 are given. The text notes that currency devaluation makes comparisons difficult, and it adds the municipal taxes collected for the district's eleven councils.
Briefly lists later charitable bodies, such as recolhimentos, asylums, the Hospício da Princesa D. Maria Amélia and several associations, and refers readers to their own entries.
The town was created by royal charter in 1744 and the municipality was set up in 1835. Porto Moniz parishes were twice attached to it, and in 1929 a move of the seat to a larger site was planned.

Work began in 1835 under Mousinho de Albuquerque and sped up under Silvestre Ribeiro. Water first passed through the Estrebarias tunnel in 1855. The old and new levadas cost almost 186 contos in total and irrigate the western Calheta parishes.

The parish was created by royal charter in 1676 to relieve the crowded Sé parish, with the chapel of Santa Luzia as its seat. The old chapel collapsed in the early 18th century, and a new church was finished around 1741.
Tristão Vaz settled Machico as seat of his captaincy; the parish was created about 1450 and covered the whole captaincy. Later church posts and their stipends are listed.

Foreign gold and silver coin circulated in Madeira, and Portuguese money was often refused. Finance minister Serpa Pimentel proposed unification in 1875, which became law on 2 May 1879 after lobbying by the Funchal Commercial Association and Madeiran parliamentarians.

Brandão led the diocese of Funchal for 26 years, and his harsh stance on the expulsion of the Jesuits was criticised. He was born at Vila Cova de Sub Avo and was appointed bishop in 1756. He arrived in Funchal on 5 August 1757.

An early church was built in the 17th century and largely rebuilt around 1735. A new church was begun in 1883, stalled for lack of funds, and was consecrated in 1918 thanks to a bequest from José de Abreu.

A milder outbreak began in October 1910. A high commissioner and Dr Carlos França were sent from Lisbon, and França directed the sanitary services. Deaths totalled 556, and the north coast and Calheta were largely spared.
Argues the fire neither lasted seven years nor covered the whole island, following Dr Azevedo in limiting it to the south.

Book II was printed in Funchal in 1873 with Azevedo's notes, from a copy obtained from the Agrela da Câmara family. Ernesto do Canto later found the copy inaccurate and corrected much of it against the autograph.

Câmara Pestana was born in Funchal in 1863, studied medicine in Lisbon and was sent to Paris in 1891 to study bacteriology and Koch's tuberculin. There he worked in leading laboratories and presented research on tetanus toxins.

The 1875 decree created four comarcas: Funchal, Ponta do Sol, São Vicente and Santa Cruz, each with its julgados de paz. Juízes ordinários were abolished in 1886, the São Vicente comarca was abolished in 1927, and a municipal julgado was set up there in 1931.

In 1533 Fernão Nunes came down from the hills claiming the Holy Spirit had sent him to preach with his paralysed niece Filipa. The people, officials and clergy believed him, and a notary who read a prayer book during a sermon was killed by the crowd.

In 1480 the land was sold to the second captain-donatary, who gave it to his daughters on entering the Santa Clara convent, hence the name. The nuns fled there during the French corsair sack of Funchal in 1560.
Paul da Serra is the only true plateau, though smaller flats are also called plateaux. The main coastal points and the principal valleys are listed.
A former public works director recalls measuring the 633-metre drop and finding that the height only became apparent when he saw a tiny fishing boat below.

Sugar was the main source of wealth in early colonisation and in 1932 all of it was made in Funchal. Alcohol is used to fortify export wines, while aguardente production was cut by law in 1927 to fight alcoholism.

Albuquerque planned to invade Egypt and divert the Nile, and he asked King Manuel to send Madeiran labourers for the task. These men were renowned for cutting levadas through the island's mountains. The account is supported by a quotation from Pinheiro Chagas.

The rules governing the new state irrigation works are set out: loans, the administrative commission, the land register, irrigators' associations and the charges landowners pay. The rules also cover the sale of hydro-electric power.

Prince Henry granted Coimbra University twelve marks of silver a year from Madeiran tithes for its chief theology professor. A friar later compiled the names of island students at Coimbra from 1578 to 1730, and 276 of them were Madeiran.
Lists the public clocks in several parishes and in Porto Santo, with who acquired or gave each one.

Isolation and economic decline helped preserve the oral poetry. Azevedo's promised Cancioneiro for Teófilo Braga was never delivered, and Leite de Vasconcelos wrote a critical article on the Romanceiro.
The parish first met in the chapel of São Tiago. A new church was rebuilt from 1753 and blessed in 1756. A curacy was created in 1731, and several chapels are listed, both surviving and lost.

Agriculture is the island's main economic base, supported by water, forests and livestock. The entry calls for forestry legislation and a forest district, and notes that livestock has only recently attracted official attention.

He spent much of his fortune on property and original buildings, including a house at Jardim da Serra where his mausoleum stands. In 1828 he helped many Madeirans, including the governor, flee to the frigate Alligator.

A quoted author says most inlayers repeat traditional motifs on small tables and boxes, many sold to ship passengers by bumboat traders. Notable pieces include a table for President Sidónio Pais and two tables ordered by the future King Luís in 1858.

The author argues that the 1932 decree on art museums did not oblige the council to change its museum, and that an art section could be attached to it. The museum opened on 5 October 1933 in the Palácio de São Pedro, mainly thanks to Adolfo César de Noronha.
Skilled machete player.
Person with an entry in the Elucidário, cross-referenced here in connection with Phelps.
Colonel who published Glover's diary in Oxford in 1931.
Portuguese compiler of the Cancioneiro Geral, which preserves the compositions of fifteenth-century Madeiran poets, including thirteen poems by João Gomes.
Lexicographer cited on the meaning of zarco.

Priest who in 1705 published at Tortona, Italy, an expanded Italian translation of D. Francisco Manuel de Melo's account of Roberto Machim's legendary discovery of Madeira. The second chapter of his book is valued for its information on Madeira in the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries.

Mainland military engineer and army captain who directed district public works in Funchal, including the Pontinha road of 1873–75, taught mathematics at the lyceum and published an 1871 map of Madeira. He died in Coimbra.
Author of the book 'A Ordem de Cristo' (1901), quoted in the Elucidário on D. João Lobo and D. Diogo Pinheiro.

Portuguese infante, later King Luís I, who first visited Madeira in 1858, when he attended the founding of the Sociedade Auxiliadora da Instrução Primária and became its protector. He commanded the corvette Bartolomeu Dias escorting the Empress of Austria on her departure in 1861.

Madeiran politician treated in the Elucidário under his title, Visconde das Nogueiras. He was clerk of the Funchal council, a journalist, and a leader of the Regenerator party and later the Fusionist party in Madeira.
Father of the bishop.
Appointed governor of the Damão fortress.
Parish priest who ceded glebe land for the seventeenth-century church.
Owner of the Quinta das Angústias who made major improvements to it.
Talented amateur actor who had performed at the Teatro Concórdia and was a founding member of the Sociedade Esperança.

D. Francisco Manuel de Melo was a 17th-century Portuguese writer, soldier and diplomat descended from Zarco's line. His third Epanaphora popularised the Machim legend of Madeira's discovery. He stopped in Madeira in 1655 on his way to exile in Brazil.

Name under which the notes group Portuguese royal figures called D. Pedro, including the prince regent who confirmed a governor of Madeira in 1668 and Pedro IV, leader of the Liberal expedition landing at Mindelo in 1832, whose constitutional cause was defended in Madeira.
Wife of Bartolomeu Perestrelo.
Previous owner of the Alecrins quinta, father of the founder.
Wife of Fernão Favila, whom she married in Madeira.
Moroccan prince whose family and household arrived at Funchal in 1793 while he sought to shelter them at Salé from civil war.
Empress Carlota of Mexico wintered in Madeira from December 1859 and called again in April 1864 with Emperor Maximilian. She is reputed to have written 'Um inverno na Madeira' (A Winter in Madeira).
King of Portugal whose charters of 26 September 1433 granted the archipelago to Prince Henry and its spiritual jurisdiction to the Order of Christ. He was the father of Infante Fernando.
Father of Juvenal Henriques de Araújo.

Madeiran physician born in Ponta do Sol, professor at the Funchal Medical-Surgical School from 1874 and its director from 1883 to 1907, and deputy for Madeira in 1885. His Elucidário entry is largely a tribute reprinted from the Heraldo da Madeira.
English merchant who settled in Funchal around 1660 and founded the Jérvis family of Madeira.
Director of the Bank of Portugal who stayed in Funchal in 1878 to settle the bankruptcy of the bank's local agent, Leitão.
Madeiran soldier who distinguished himself in Brazil in the wars against the Dutch.
Clerk of the Funchal municipal secretariat from 1835 who compiled manuscript genealogical notes on Madeiran families in 1887–88, held by the library.
Wife of the dramatist, mother of his seven children.
Desembargador who in 1683 investigated accusations against the provedor and treasury officials.
The 22nd bishop of Funchal, whose troubled episcopate spanned the liberal–absolutist conflicts of 1820–1834. He left Madeira in 1834 and died in exile in Genoa.
First canonically instituted parish priest of Quinta Grande, in 1862.
F. de Assis Sousa Vaz was a physician who published a treatise in Paris in 1832 praising Madeira's climate for treating pulmonary tuberculosis. He wrote it without visiting the island.
Governor and viceroy of Portuguese India and brother-in-law of João Rodrigues de Noronha.
Genealogist who traced the Zarco family back to the twelfth century and explained the name as meaning green-eyed. In unpublished work he denied that the Câmara name derived from seals.
One of five constitutionalists who demanded the proclamation on 5 June 1834.
Lombo de Dona Isabel is a locality in Santo António parish, Funchal, and has its own Elucidário entry. It is a slope on the access route to Curral das Freiras and neighbours Vasco Gil.

Funchal's municipal theatre, built with a loan by the council on the former convent grounds and the site of the 1823 market. Begun in 1884 and inaugurated in 1888 as Teatro D. Maria Pia, it was renamed after Manuel de Arriaga in 1921. It hosted revues such as A Madeira por dentro, lectures and concerts, including the 1921 orfeão.

The Levada de D. Isabel, also called the Fundoa levada, is a private levada in Funchal and a founding member of the Liga das Levadas. It is fed partly by springs of the Montado do Barreiro and irrigates São Roque, São Pedro and Santa Luzia.
Chapel that gave the locality its name.

The Paul da Serra is the only extensive plateau on Madeira, lying at about 1,500 m across four municipalities, where temperatures can fall to freezing. The Rabaçal and Risco springs, the Ribeira da Tabua and the Ribeira da Janela rise at its edges, and it feeds the main levadas. The Elucidário records its vegetation, agricultural trials, shelter houses, sheep-shearing gatherings, common-land use and an unfinished road project.

Rua dos Aranhas is a Funchal street named after the Aranha family who lived there, and was formerly called Rua do Dr. Chaves. It contains the Casa de Dona Mécia and a surviving Gothic house of the Ornelas family. It was the site of the Anglican church opened in 1848, the Escola Normal and the Teatro Esperança, and the São Lázaro gate stood at its top until 1904.
Fonte is a locality in Monte parish, Funchal, where the Largo da Fonte lies. It was the site of an intermediate station of the Monte railway.
One of the island's principal springs.
Forests damaged.

Rua do Bispo is the former name of Rua de Gomes Freire in Funchal, named after the bishops' residence and episcopal palace that stood there. Bishop D. Frei João do Nascimento died in a house on this street that later held the lyceum. The street also housed the Clube Recreio e Instrução and the «Vicente» photographic studio, and it was hit by a shell in 1916.
The Quinta de Sant'Ana is an estate in Monte parish, Funchal, granted to Dr João Francisco de Oliveira in 1803. The Furna do Cavalum lies nearby.
Atalhinho is a sítio in the parish of Monte, Funchal. The Monte railway reached it in 1894, and it formed one end of a section of the line.

Torres Vedras is a Portuguese mainland town. The revolt of February 1844 broke out there, and Luís da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque received his fatal wound in a clash there. The nearby Fonte Nova spring was cited as a mainland water comparable to that of São Roque.
Cape Verde island to which an old decree ordered lepers sent.
Guesthouse where Nobre lived, later the Atlantic Hotel.
One of the chapels in the parish.
Cumiada Alta is a high ridge on Madeira, rising above 1,700 metres near Pico Ruivo and the basalt column known as Homem em Pé. The Elucidário notes it for its rare plants.

Ponta do Pargo is a parish at Madeira's western extremity, transferred from Porto do Moniz to Calheta municipality in 1871, where a lighthouse long demanded was first lit in 1922. It is watered by the old Rabaçal levada, grows Sercial vines, gives its name to a white cattle sub-breed, and was the birthplace of Manuel da Costa Dias and João Pestana Júnior.

Old public promenade in Funchal, the name of the later Praça da Constituição before 1821, with a bandstand used in celebrations. The garrison declared for the revolution there on 29 April 1847, and Popular partisans tried to kill Dr Trindade e Vasconcelos there. The Teatro de Bom Gosto also had access onto it.
House where passengers did quarantine, probably near Praia Formosa.
His birthplace.

The Ilhéu da Rocha do Navio is an islet off the coast of Santana, near the Rocha do Navio locality. A Dutch ship was wrecked there in 1860. The islet is also used to situate the nearby Ponta do Cortado.

Vila is the main locality of the parish of Porto do Moniz and seat of the municipality, with the town hall, other municipal offices, the parish church and a cemetery. It is commonly but improperly called 'Vila', never having been formally raised to town status.
Vila is an inhabited locality on Porto Santo comprising the island's town and its surroundings.

Ribeira de Santa Cruz is a stream that rises at Santo António da Serra and flows through Santa Cruz to the sea. Its chief tributary is the Ribeira da Serra de Água, and it has the Madre de Água waterfall. The name also denotes a locality of the parish.
Place of publication of his work.
The Teatro Grande was a theatre in Funchal where Oliveira Paixão played. It was demolished in 1832 on the orders of D. Álvaro da Costa de Sousa Macedo because liberals used it for propaganda.
Three former chapels dedicated to Santa Quitéria in Madeira. They stood at Pico do Cardo in Santo António parish (1727), at Lombo da Estrela in Calheta (1724), and at Madalena do Mar.
Native origin of the shrub.
A brief account of early attempts to light the coasts of Madeira. It notes in particular an unsuccessful parliamentary bill of 1861 for lighthouses at Ponta de São Lourenço and on the Pontinha islet.

The Rua da Saúde is a street in Funchal, and before 1838 its name was used for what became the Entrada da Cidade. Works on the Saúde gate and street were authorised in 1838 and begun in 1839. The name, taken from the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Saúde that stands on it, survives in the rua and calçada da Saúde, which are linked by the Rua das Mercês.

Rua das Mercês is a Funchal street named after the former Convent of Mercês, which stood on it and was demolished from 1911. It was the second site of the military hospital, is joined by Rua do Castanheiro, and once included the Rua dos Moinhos.

Rua do Príncipe was the former name of a Funchal street running alongside the Ribeira de Santa Luzia, from the Calçada do Cidrão to the Rua dos Netos. It was renamed Rua 5 de Outubro after the proclamation of the Republic. The name probably honoured the Prince Regent D. João VI, though no municipal record confirms this; the street lay at the other end of the present rua and calçada da Saúde.
Principal locality.
One of the parish's main localities.

The Chapel of Our Lady of Loreto, at Lombada do Loreto in Arco da Calheta, was founded by Pedro Gonçalves da Câmara, son of the second captain-donatary, and was reportedly built in 1510. It later became the seat of an entailed estate and was the centre of an annual pilgrimage.
The parish church of Calheta, located in the Vila locality.
First military commander of Madeira after the separation of civil and military offices in 1834.
Author of 'Tocares e Cantares da Ilha' (Funchal, 1937), which contains a chapter on the charamba.
Ran private singing and piano courses in Funchal, later piano professor at the Lisbon Conservatory until 1921.
Namesake of the avenue formerly called Avenida Oeste.
Moura's predecessor as bishop of Funchal, transferred to Guarda in 1858.
Bishop of Funchal who made Madalena do Mar an independent parish on 1 February 1582.
Drew a map of Madeira that, according to Stuebel, represents its topographic-genetic structure well.
One of the first teachers of the Funchal teacher-training school in 1900.
Author of Saudades da Terra (1590), praising Madeira malmsey as the world's best.
Engineer who completed the general map of Madeira begun by Oudinot.
Dutch prince who came to Madeira in 1847 and died there in 1848.
Coimbra law graduate (1874) who practised as a distinguished advocate in Madeira.
Chronicler of the Saudades da Terra, cited as source for the family.
Reached ensign in the Liberal army.
King who gave the parish church its ebony and silver tabernacle.
Ensign commanding the 30-man Miguelist detachment sent to Porto Santo in May 1832.
First Philippine governor-general of Madeira, who became treasury provedor in 1582.
Father of Maria Clementina, at whose wish she took the veil at Santa Clara.
Fifteenth-century Portuguese chronicler who wrote the name as 'Machito'.
Madeiran-born author listed among writers of the third quarter of the nineteenth century.
Early vicar of Porto da Cruz.
One of five constitutionalists who demanded the proclamation on 5 June 1834.
Discoverer and captain of Funchal, founder in 1450 of the entail of the Calheta counts.
Built the Bom Sucesso chapel in 1683.
Mother of João António Monteiro.
Naturalist who found jaws of a small vertebrate among the Piedade calcareous deposits.
Madeiran-born prelate who was bishop of Funchal and archbishop of Goa.
Jesuit author cited as recounting the tradition.
Azorean chronicler, author of Saudades da Terra, quoted describing the chapel and a legend about it.
Madeiran friend of Nobre, author of 'Coimbra nos Noventas...', who encouraged him to come to Madeira.
Civil governor of Madeira whom Nery attacked violently from the pulpit of the Carmo church in his presence.
Madeiran pharmacist at the Estefânia hospital in Lisbon and author of the pamphlet Em Lisboa.
Funchal industrialist who offered tea at his residence to Norton de Matos's party in 1921.
Baritone.
Peer of the realm created Baron of São Pedro in 1845.
Civil engineer and brother of Adriano Augusto Trigo, who collaborated on five of his works.
Funchal-born Franciscan friar and renowned preacher in Lisbon, subject of this entry.
The parish containing the locality of Boliqueme.
Its port lies about 41 miles from Funchal.
Feast of Nossa Senhora do Livramento, known for strings of dried pears.
Street forming part of the parish boundary.
Site of fossil snail deposits.
Stream on whose left bank the church stood and whose floods destroyed it.
Diocese where he served as vicar general from 1824.
Garden flanked on the west by the street.
His birthplace and the comarca where he served as registrar.
The island Moquet visited in 1601 and wrote about.
Canary island whose natives were barred from residing in Madeira in 1490.
Levada from Santa Cruz irrigating the parish.
Parish from which São Martinho was separated in 1579.
The island whose flora and fauna are the subject of this entry.
The seaplane flew as far as this area on 28 March 1921.
The Desertas island on whose west coast the Porto da Alagoa lies.
Its cuttings show peaks buried by lavas.
Homeland of André Gonçalves de França.
Final resting place of Bishop Figueiredo de Lemos's remains.
Upland site celebrated for its lagoon, great trees and scenery.
Seat of the França and Reis Magos entails.
Canary island covered in one of Bunbury's botanical papers.
Existing chapel that became the parish church and was enlarged around 1699.
The locality described in this entry.
Birthplace of Adriano Augusto Trigo.
Estate bought by the company, housing a sanatorium building.
Capital of the captaincy from which Calheta was separated.
Home of a large Moorish community and a Moorish quarter.
Chapel that gave the locality its name.
Site of a state-owned levada.
Parish overlooked by the Cortado viewpoint.
Chapel damaged in 1748 and later restored.
Highest point of Madeira, 1861 m.
Birthplace of the jurist.
Where a later edition of his book appeared.
Where Knowler gave his lectures.
Parish crossed by the path along the levada.
António Gil Gomes returned to Madeira after representative government was established.
He died in Ponta do Sol.
Modern export of Madeiran sugar began, according to Dr. Azevedo.
The 9th Military Division was created in Madeira.
An earthquake badly damaged the Calheta São José chapel.
Gil de Carvalho built a small hermitage, probably dedicated to Saint Anthony, at Alcoforado.
The cortes were dissolved and absolute government restored.
The first newspaper A Madeira Liberal was published, issuing sixteen numbers.
A collection of poems offered to Sebastião Xavier Botelho, including works by Atouguia, was published in Funchal.
Leal represented Madeira in the Portuguese parliament.
Gaula's fifteenth-century silver cross was shown at the Lisbon Retrospective Exhibition of Ornamental Art.
Regimento removed all exemptions from the finto.
Election riots broke out, with several people shot dead by troops at Ribeira Brava.
Francisco José Rodrigues de Andrade was born.
He died at Raudamy castle.
Boundary disputes between Santa Cruz and Machico over the area ended.
Wine production fell to only 600 hectolitres.
Regulations for the brandy resale tax were issued.
The Tybumia fled Funchal by night to avoid customs, fired on by the Ilhéu fortress.
German wine law regulating Madeira wine imports.
The poet known as Manuel Ribeiro was born in Lisbon.
Several civil governors succeeded one another in the year of the Republic's proclamation.
The second newspaper O Povo was published, issuing 1248 numbers until 30 September 1917.
The archdiocese of Funchal was created with four suffragan dioceses, making the cathedral an archiepiscopal see.
Manuel II was acclaimed king in Funchal, without the customary procession.
Governor D. José Manuel da Câmara visited the Palheiro property and attended the laying of the doorsteps.
Governor Travassos Valdez began the Porto Novo fort.
Prince Henry issued donation letters for the three captaincies to the first captains.
Many Madeirans visited Santa Cruz de Tenerife and were warmly received.
A terrace was built over the Funchal post.
The interim commission's administration of the treasury ended.
Death of King Manuel I.
